questions.prompt: What changes when the membrane pattern is divided into more oppositely moving regions?
questions.answer: More divisions produce more internal nodes between oppositely moving regions. The outside edges remain fixed.
rubric: Identify additional internal stationary boundaries.

options.text: Its outside edges become free.
options.feedback: The outside edges remain fixed across the displayed membrane modes.

options.text: Its whole surface moves in one direction together.
options.feedback: That describes a broad single-region movement rather than additional alternating regions.

options.text: It has more internal stationary boundaries.
options.feedback: Oppositely moving regions are separated by nodes, so additional regions introduce more internal boundaries.

options.text: Its frequency components turn into separate pieces of material.
options.feedback: Modes describe movements of the same membrane, not separate material pieces.

questions.prompt: Where are the displacement node and antinode in the fixed–free string?
questions.answer: The fixed end is a displacement node, and the free end is a displacement antinode.
rubric: Match the stationary node to the fixed end and the antinode to the free end.

options.text: Antinode at the fixed end; node at the free end.
options.feedback: This reverses the endpoint restrictions.

options.text: Node at the fixed end; antinode at the free end.
options.feedback: The fixed end cannot move, while the free end has a large movement over the cycle.

options.text: Nodes at both ends.
options.feedback: That would describe two fixed ends rather than the displayed fixed–free condition.

options.text: Antinodes at both ends.
options.feedback: The fixed end must remain stationary.

questions.prompt: The fundamental is 100 Hz. Which label fits the second allowed fixed–free mode?
questions.answer: It is the third harmonic at 300 Hz. Mode number counts allowed patterns, while harmonic number compares frequency with the fundamental.
rubric: Distinguish second mode from third harmonic.

options.text: Second harmonic, 200 Hz.
options.feedback: The second harmonic would not satisfy the displayed node–antinode endpoint pattern.

options.text: Third harmonic, 300 Hz.
options.feedback: The allowed sequence is 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz; the second mode is three times the fundamental.

options.text: First harmonic, 100 Hz.
options.feedback: That labels the first allowed mode, not the second.

options.text: Fourth harmonic, 400 Hz.
options.feedback: The fourth harmonic is even and is not the second allowed fixed–free pattern.

questions.prompt: Why do the fixed–free patterns fit 1, 3, 5, and 7 quarter-waves?
questions.answer: An odd number of quarter-waves connects a node to an antinode. That matches the fixed and free endpoints.
rubric: Connect the odd counts to the required endpoint types.

options.text: Odd counts put displacement nodes at both ends.
options.feedback: An even quarter-wave count would connect two nodes; the free end requires an antinode.

options.text: Odd counts connect the fixed-end node to the free-end antinode.
options.feedback: Adding a pair of quarter-waves preserves the different endpoint types.

options.text: Each quarter-wave turns the whole string into a separate oscillator.
options.feedback: The pieces divide one standing-wave shape rather than independent strings.

options.text: The missing counts would require a longer string.
options.feedback: The deciding restriction is the endpoint pattern, not an inability to fit an even count into a length.

questions.prompt: Which motion do the circles represent in the air-column model?
questions.answer: They move longitudinally, back and forth along the tube.
rubric: Identify lengthwise oscillation.

options.text: Sideways motion across the tube.
options.feedback: That would confuse the air motion with the transverse string drawing.

options.text: A steady stream from the glottis to the lips.
options.feedback: The elements reverse direction instead of flowing continuously outward.

options.text: Back-and-forth motion along the tube.
options.feedback: The model shows longitudinal air movement around usual positions.

options.text: A stationary row whose gaps never change.
options.feedback: The sampled phases show movement and changing spacing.

questions.prompt: Several neighboring air elements move together while their gaps stay almost unchanged. What is strong there?
questions.answer: The region has strong movement but little changing compression. Movement and spacing must be tracked separately.
rubric: Separate the group’s movement from its nearly unchanged spacing.

options.text: Air movement, with little change in local compression.
options.feedback: The group travels, but nearly unchanged spacing means little density change within it.

options.text: Compression, with little air movement.
options.feedback: Large travel of the elements is movement; compression requires changing spacing.

options.text: A new fixed boundary.
options.feedback: Moving together does not create a stationary endpoint.

options.text: No acoustic movement, because the neighboring gaps stay constant.
options.feedback: The elements are moving even when the gaps within the group change little.

questions.prompt: How are the vowels in dean and dune alike and different in the tract comparison?
questions.answer: Both are high vowels. Dean is front with a front narrowing, while dune is back with a highlighted lip narrowing.
rubric: Identify shared high position and different front/back and narrowing locations.

options.text: Both are front; their main difference is that dune is low.
options.feedback: Dune is the high-back example in this comparison.

options.text: Both are low; dean has the lip narrowing.
options.feedback: Dean is high-front, and the highlighted lip narrowing belongs to dune.

options.text: Both use the central, unconstricted reference shape.
options.feedback: Done supplies that reference, rather than dean or dune.

options.text: Both are high; dean is front and dune is back, with different narrowing locations.
options.feedback: The shared height does not make the front and lip constrictions the same.

questions.prompt: Why can one constriction raise one formant and lower another?
questions.answer: Each mode places movement and compression differently. The mass effect can matter most for one and the stiffness effect for another.
rubric: Explain the different local roles of the same constriction across modes.

options.text: The mass rule reverses for the second mode.
options.feedback: More effective mass still tends to lower frequency where movement matters.

options.text: The constriction changes its position between the two modes.
options.feedback: The position can stay fixed while its role within each mode differs.

options.text: Its mass and stiffness changes cancel equally in each mode.
options.feedback: Equal cancellation would not explain the different formant shifts.

options.text: The two modes move and compress the affected region differently.
options.feedback: The same location can emphasize inertia for one mode and restoring stiffness for another.

questions.prompt: In the /u/ lip-loading model, which way do F1 and F2 change?
questions.answer: F1 and F2 both fall.
rubric: Give both downward directions.

options.text: F1 rises; F2 rises.
options.feedback: That would require stiffness to dominate both effects, unlike the shown lip-loading explanation.

options.text: F1 falls; F2 falls.
options.feedback: Both modes move strongly near the lips, so the added mass effect lowers both resonances.

options.text: F1 falls; F2 rises.
options.feedback: That is the front-constriction pattern, not the lip-loading pattern.

options.text: F1 rises; F2 falls.
options.feedback: That is the back-constriction pattern, not the lip-loading pattern.

questions.prompt: Why does F2 rise in the front /i/ constriction model?
questions.answer: The front region contributes strongly to compression in Mode 2. The stronger restoring response raises F2.
rubric: Connect Mode 2 compression to the stronger restoring response and higher F2.

options.text: The constriction adds mass where Mode 2 moves most strongly.
options.feedback: A dominant mass effect would lower the resonance.

options.text: The vocal folds switch to the second harmonic.
options.feedback: F2 is a tract resonance, not the second source harmonic.

options.text: The front narrowing moves to the lip end for Mode 2.
options.feedback: The same front location is changed in both rows.

options.text: The constriction strengthens the restoring response in a strongly compressing region of Mode 2.
options.feedback: The spring-like effect makes the cycle faster there.

questions.prompt: Which formant pattern belongs to the back /a/ constriction model?
questions.answer: F1 rises and F2 falls.
rubric: Give the upward F1 and downward F2 directions.

options.text: F1 rises; F2 falls.
options.feedback: Stiffness matters most for Mode 1 there, while the mass effect matters most for Mode 2.

options.text: F1 falls; F2 rises.
options.feedback: That is the front /i/ pattern.

options.text: F1 falls; F2 falls.
options.feedback: That is the /u/ lip-loading pattern.

options.text: F1 rises; F2 rises.
options.feedback: The model gives a dominant mass effect that lowers the second resonance.

questions.prompt: If F0 rises while the vowel filter stays the same, what happens to the source harmonics?
questions.answer: The harmonics become farther apart, leaving fewer components within the same frequency window.
rubric: Link higher F0 to wider harmonic spacing.

options.text: They become farther apart.
options.feedback: Neighboring source harmonics are separated by F0, so a larger F0 widens the gaps.

options.text: They become more closely spaced.
options.feedback: Closer spacing would correspond to a lower source fundamental.

options.text: They shift to the formant targets and lose their regular spacing.
options.feedback: The source still sets harmonic locations; the filter changes relative strengths.

options.text: Their spacing stays fixed while each formant moves upward.
options.feedback: The filter is held fixed in the question, while F0 controls source spacing.

questions.prompt: What does the vocal-tract filter chiefly change in the source–filter comparison?
questions.answer: It changes the relative strengths of the source harmonics according to the tract’s resonance regions.
rubric: Identify relative harmonic strength as the filter effect.

options.text: The number of vocal-fold cycles per second.
options.feedback: That is the source fundamental’s role in this comparison.

options.text: The meaning of the spectrum’s frequency axis.
options.feedback: The axis still represents frequency in the same units.

options.text: The source harmonic spacing to match every formant gap.
options.feedback: Formant targets and harmonic spacing are separate properties.

options.text: The relative strengths of the source harmonics.
options.feedback: Resonances favor nearby components and weaken others relative to them.

questions.prompt: A formant target lies between two source harmonics. What can happen?
questions.answer: The nearby harmonics can be emphasized. A filter resonance does not require a source component at precisely its target frequency.
rubric: Keep a filter target distinct from actual source harmonic locations.

options.text: Nearby harmonics can be strengthened even without a harmonic exactly at the target.
options.feedback: A resonance region can favor components on either side of its target.

options.text: The source must add a new harmonic at the target.
options.feedback: The source frequencies remain determined by F0.

options.text: The filter target must move onto the nearest harmonic.
options.feedback: A sparse source does not require the tract resonance to move.

options.text: That resonance stops affecting the sound.
options.feedback: Nearby source components can still be affected by its filter region.

questions.prompt: A spectrogram band moves upward. What does that movement mean?
questions.answer: The band moves to a higher frequency.
rubric: Read upward position as higher frequency.

options.text: Its amplitude increases.
options.feedback: Amplitude is represented by darkness, not vertical position.

options.text: Its frequency increases.
options.feedback: Frequency is vertical in this spectrogram.

options.text: The sound occurs later.
options.feedback: Time advances horizontally, rather than upward.

options.text: Its frequency decreases.
options.feedback: A lower frequency would place the band lower on this spectrogram.

questions.prompt: A band gets darker at the same spectrogram height. What changes?
questions.answer: The component becomes stronger at the same frequency.
rubric: Read darkness as amplitude while holding frequency fixed.

options.text: Its frequency increases.
options.feedback: A frequency increase would move the band upward.

options.text: It occurs later without becoming stronger.
options.feedback: Later time lies farther right; darkness encodes strength.

options.text: It becomes a lower-frequency resonance.
options.feedback: A lower frequency would put the band lower, not simply make it darker.

options.text: Its amplitude increases at that frequency.
options.feedback: The black–gray–white scale represents amplitude, while unchanged height means unchanged frequency.

questions.prompt: What are the two measured inputs to the vowel network?
questions.answer: F1 and F2.
rubric: Identify the two formant inputs.

options.text: F1 and F2.
options.feedback: The model starts from the first two formant measurements.

options.text: F0 and speaking duration.
options.feedback: Those are not the two labelled inputs in this architecture.

options.text: The true vowel and its predicted vowel.
options.feedback: Those are category labels, not the two input measurements.

options.text: The largest two output probabilities.
options.feedback: Outputs follow the hidden layers; they are not the initial formant inputs.

questions.prompt: One first-hidden-layer neuron receives F1 and F2. How many incoming weights does it have?
questions.answer: Two, one for each incoming formant value.
rubric: Count one weight per incoming connection.

options.text: One.
options.feedback: Combining two inputs does not make them share one incoming connection weight.

options.text: Three.
options.feedback: Three is the number of receiving neurons in that layer, not the incoming count for one neuron.

options.text: Two.
options.feedback: Each of the two incoming connections has its own weight.

options.text: Five.
options.feedback: Five is the final output count, not this neuron’s incoming connection count.

questions.prompt: How does a neuron combine its incoming values in this linear network?
questions.answer: It multiplies each incoming value by that connection’s weight and adds the products.
rubric: Describe weighting each input and summing the resulting contributions.

options.text: Add the input values, then choose the largest weight.
options.feedback: The displayed network uses a separate weighted contribution from each connection.

options.text: Multiply the weights together and discard the inputs.
options.feedback: The input measurements take part in the weighted sums.

options.text: Use whichever input has the highest numerical value.
options.feedback: The neuron combines incoming weighted values rather than selecting the largest raw input.

options.text: Multiply each value by its own weight, then add the products.
options.feedback: This forms the receiving neuron’s weighted sum.

questions.prompt: What do the random starting weights tell us about the network’s vowel knowledge?
questions.answer: They describe the untrained starting configuration. Labels and random weights do not establish learned recognition.
rubric: Distinguish random initialization from knowledge acquired through training.

options.text: The named outputs show that all five vowels have already been learned.
options.feedback: An output label states its intended meaning; it does not establish successful recognition.

options.text: The positive connections already contain the correct vowel labels.
options.feedback: A weight’s sign controls its contribution, not a known correct category.

options.text: The first forward pass has already trained the connections.
options.feedback: Using current weights to produce an output does not itself update them.

options.text: They give a starting configuration, not learned vowel knowledge.
options.feedback: Learning would require changing those settings using examples.

questions.prompt: Which change would be learning rather than just a forward pass?
questions.answer: Learning changes the weights using feedback, whereas a forward pass uses the current weights.
rubric: Distinguish a parameter update from processing an input with fixed parameters.

options.text: Passing a new formant pair through unchanged weights.
options.feedback: That produces another output with the current model.

options.text: Changing connection weights using feedback about examples.
options.feedback: Learning changes the settings that future forward passes use.

options.text: Reading the largest current output bar.
options.feedback: Interpreting an output does not itself alter any weight.

options.text: Passing hidden-layer results to the next layer.
options.feedback: That is part of forward information flow with the current weights.

questions.prompt: Which list could be a probability distribution across four alternatives?
questions.answer: The valid list is [0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.4]. Its entries are nonnegative and add to one.
rubric: Require valid individual probabilities and a total of one.

options.feedback: These entries add to zero rather than one.
A probability cannot be negative, even when the entries add to one.
The entries are between zero and one and add to one.
These entries add to more than one.

questions.prompt: In the illustrated output, which label has the largest probability bar?
questions.answer: /done/ has the largest illustrated bar.
rubric: Read the largest bar with its correct output label.

options.text: /dean/.
options.feedback: Its illustrated bar is 0.1, not the largest.

options.text: /dune/.
options.feedback: Its illustrated bar is 0.1, not the largest.

options.text: /done/.
options.feedback: Its illustrated value is 0.5, larger than /Dan/ at 0.2 and the others at 0.1.

options.text: /Dan/.

questions.prompt: What does bias=False remove from a Linear layer?
questions.answer: It removes the added bias offset, not the connection weights.
rubric: Identify the removed constant offset without freezing or removing weights.

options.text: An extra constant added to each weighted sum.
options.feedback: It removes the bias offset, while the connection weights remain.

options.text: The weights on negative connections.
options.feedback: The argument does not remove weights according to their signs.

options.text: The ability of its weights to change during training.
options.feedback: Removing a bias does not freeze the connection weights.

options.text: The incoming measurements themselves.
options.feedback: The layer still receives and combines its inputs.

questions.prompt: What does nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False) specify?
questions.answer: It defines a layer receiving two values and producing three weighted sums.
rubric: Read the input and output counts in their correct order.

options.text: Three incoming values and two outgoing sums.
options.feedback: That reverses the input and output arguments.

options.text: Two formants and three known correct categories.
options.feedback: The three outputs of this layer are hidden values, not supplied correct labels.

options.text: Two incoming values and three outgoing weighted sums.
options.feedback: The first number is input width, and the second is output width.

options.text: Two training examples processed for three learning steps.
options.feedback: The arguments specify layer dimensions, not training counts.

questions.prompt: How can two membrane modes reinforce or partly cancel each other?
questions.answer: Their movements add at each point. Movements in the same direction reinforce, while movements in opposite directions partly cancel. As their phases change, the combined shape changes.
rubric: Explain addition of movements at the same position.
Connect same and opposite directions to reinforcement and cancellation.

questions.prompt: Why do equal spectral peaks at one membrane pickup not imply equal movement everywhere?
questions.answer: The pickup records movement at one position. Different modes move that position and other positions by different amounts. The amplitudes were adjusted to give equal readings at the chosen pickup.
rubric: Identify the measurement as position-specific.
Explain why changing position changes the relative modal contributions.

questions.prompt: Keep length and wave speed fixed. What happens to the fundamental when a fixed–fixed string becomes fixed–free?
questions.answer: It falls to half its former frequency. The changed endpoint allows the lowest pattern to fit as a quarter-wave rather than a half-wave. Separately retuned examples with matching labels do not isolate this boundary change.
rubric: Give the halving under the stated controls.
Connect the changed allowed pattern to the changed fundamental.

questions.prompt: Can a displacement antinode pass through its resting position? Explain.
questions.answer: Yes. An antinode identifies a location with a large movement over a cycle, not a point that stays at maximum displacement. It passes through its resting position on the way from one side to the other.
rubric: Interpret an antinode over a cycle.
Distinguish zero displacement at an instant from a stationary node.

questions.prompt: Why do higher fixed–free modes repeat faster in the same string length?
questions.answer: They fit more quarter-waves into that length, so their wavelengths are shorter. With wave speed unchanged, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a faster repetition.
rubric: Connect more fitted pieces to shorter wavelengths.
Relate shorter wavelength to higher frequency with fixed wave speed.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish air movement from changing compression in the animation?
questions.answer: Track one element to see how far it moves back and forth. Compare the gaps between neighbors to see compression and expansion. A group can move together without much change in its internal spacing.
rubric: Use one element’s movement to assess movement.
Use changing neighbor spacing to assess compression.
questions.topic: Observing two aspects of air vibration

questions.prompt: Dean and dune are both high vowels. Why can their formant patterns still differ?
questions.answer: Their narrowings occur at different places: the front region for dean and the lips for dune. Each place affects the modes’ movement and compression differently. Sharing tongue height therefore does not require the same resonances.
rubric: Identify different narrowing locations despite shared height.
Connect location to different effects on air-mode patterns.
questions.topic: Shared vowel height and different acoustics

questions.prompt: Why does moving the model’s narrowing from the /i/ location to the /a/ location reverse the F1 and F2 directions?
questions.answer: The two locations have different roles within each mode. At the front /i/ location, mass matters most for Mode 1 and stiffness for Mode 2; at the back /a/ location, those roles reverse. The mass and stiffness rules stay the same, but their local importance changes.
rubric: Compare the local mass and stiffness roles at the two locations.
Keep the physical rules unchanged while explaining the reversed formant pattern.

questions.prompt: Why does lip loading lower both formants in the /u/ model?
questions.answer: Both modes have strong movement near the open lip end. Added effective mass makes that movement harder to reverse, so each cycle takes longer. Both resonances therefore become lower.
rubric: Identify strong lip-region movement in both modes.
Explain greater inertia and slower cycles as the cause of both decreases.

questions.prompt: Does the air-column animation require particles to travel continuously from the glottis out of the mouth?
questions.answer: No. The elements move back and forth around their usual positions. Their changing movement and spacing represent the acoustic oscillation, rather than a steady stream of the same particles through the tube.
rubric: Identify back-and-forth movement around usual positions.
Distinguish acoustic oscillation from steady outward particle flow.

questions.prompt: What stays fixed, and what changes, when the source–filter grid moves down one vowel column?
questions.answer: The vowel filter and its formant targets stay fixed. F0 changes, which changes the spacing of the source harmonics. Their strengths sample the same filter at different frequency positions.
rubric: Identify the fixed vowel filter and formant targets.
Identify changing F0 and harmonic spacing.

questions.prompt: Why can a high-F0 source make two close formants harder to distinguish?
questions.answer: Higher F0 leaves wider gaps between harmonics. Fewer components describe the filter near its two targets, so their separate shapes can be hard to see. This does not mean that either tract resonance has disappeared.
rubric: Connect higher F0 to sparse harmonic sampling.
Explain loss of visible detail without asserting a physical resonance loss.

questions.prompt: Is a voiced vowel a vibration at one frequency? Explain using the source and filter.
questions.answer: No. The source supplies several harmonic components. The vocal tract changes their relative strengths around its resonances, producing a pattern across frequencies rather than a single tone.
rubric: Reject the single-frequency account of a voiced vowel.
Connect multiple source harmonics to filtering by tract resonances.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a source harmonic and a formant?
questions.answer: A harmonic is a frequency component supplied by the repeating source. A formant is a resonance region favored by the vocal tract. A formant can lie between harmonics and still strengthen nearby components.
rubric: Distinguish a source component from a tract resonance region.
Allow resonance targets between actual source harmonics.

questions.prompt: How would a louder component at the same frequency differ from a higher-frequency component on this spectrogram?
questions.answer: A stronger component becomes darker at the same height. A higher-frequency component moves upward. Darkness represents amplitude, while vertical position represents frequency.
rubric: Use darkness for amplitude at fixed frequency.
Use upward position for higher frequency.

questions.prompt: In the /i/ to /a/ spectrogram transition, which way do the first two strong bands move?
questions.answer: The first rises and the second falls.
rubric: Identify rising F1 and falling F2 in the pictured transition.

questions.prompt: Why is using F1 and F2 as inputs different from giving the network the true vowel label?
questions.answer: F1 and F2 are measurements describing the sound. The true label states which category that example belongs to. The network’s recognition task is to relate the measured pattern to a category.
rubric: Separate acoustic measurements from a known category.
Identify recognition as a mapping from measurements to candidate labels.

questions.prompt: The first hidden layer has three neurons, each connected to F1 and F2. How many incoming weights does that layer have?
questions.answer: Six: two incoming weights for each of its three neurons.
rubric: Count one separate weight per connection, giving six across the layer.

questions.prompt: The second hidden layer has two neurons. Are those two values new measurements of F1 and F2?
questions.answer: No. They are intermediate weighted combinations produced by the preceding layer. Their number does not make them the original measured formants again.
rubric: Distinguish computed hidden values from measured input features.
Avoid assigning input meanings merely because a hidden layer has two units.

questions.prompt: What can changing one connection weight change, even when F1 and F2 stay the same?
questions.answer: It changes that incoming value’s contribution to its receiving neuron. The resulting value can then affect later layers. It does not directly replace the measured inputs or change every other weight.
rubric: Identify the connection-specific change in a weighted contribution.
Follow its possible effect through later layers without changing unrelated parameters.

questions.prompt: Why can two first-hidden-layer neurons give different results for the same formant pair?
questions.answer: They have separate weights on their incoming connections. Each neuron multiplies the formant values by its own weights and adds the products. Different weights can therefore make different combinations of the same input.
rubric: Identify separate incoming weights for the receiving neurons.
Explain separate weighted sums of the same inputs.
questions.topic: Different combinations of one input pair

questions.prompt: A candidate probability list adds to one but contains a negative value. Is it valid? Why?
questions.answer: No. Each probability must lie between zero and one. A correct total does not make a negative entry valid.
rubric: Require valid individual entries as well as a total of one.

questions.prompt: Does the largest output bar tell us whether the network’s prediction is correct?
questions.answer: It identifies the candidate the network favors. To judge correctness, the example’s true category must also be known. The largest bar alone does not supply that target.
rubric: Distinguish the favored prediction from an independently known true category.
Require the true label to evaluate correctness.

questions.prompt: Why must the output count of one Linear layer match the next layer’s input count?
questions.answer: The next layer receives the values produced by the preceding layer. Its expected input width must match that set of values for the sequence to pass information between them.
rubric: Connect matching widths to passing the preceding layer’s output values onward.

questions.prompt: Does declaring the shown PyTorch sequence demonstrate that the network has learned vowels?
questions.answer: No. It defines the layers and their connections. Demonstrating learning would require training that changes the weights using examples, followed by evidence of what the resulting model can recognize.
rubric: Distinguish an architecture declaration from training.
Identify weight changes using examples as part of learning.
